performers: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande; Ernest Ansermet, conductor
intro: Clarinets and bassoons rock slowly beneath a recurring cor anglais phrase in Nuages, the first of Debussy’s three Nocturnes. A flute and harp briefly let in a different light.

sections.label: A · Rocking chords, cor anglais
sections.mNote: The cor anglais phrase returns above slow wind chords

sections.label: B · Flute and harp in F♯
sections.mNote: A five-note melody floats over held, divided strings

sections.label: A′ · The cor anglais returns
sections.mNote: The opening phrase comes back above quiet lower strings

sections.label: Coda · Wind fragments and plucked strings
sections.mNote: Short wind phrases linger over the last pizzicato notes

cues.title: Clarinets and bassoons
cues.text: Clarinets and bassoons begin alone, rocking slowly between chords. The strings have nothing to play yet. An oboe adds a held note, then a small falling phrase, while the chords continue underneath.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, Kalmus reprint, printed p. 2, opening four bars: clarinets and bassoons, then oboe. https://purl.dlib.indiana.edu/iudl/variations/score/BFJ7336
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The cor anglais phrase
cues.text: The cor anglais has a phrase that keeps coming back with almost the same shape. Its dry, slightly nasal voice sits apart from the soft chords around it. Debussy lets it return without growing into a long song.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, opening section and return, printed pp. 3–4 and 16. The cor anglais phrase is a recurring feature of the movement.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Whistler’s borrowed word
cues.text: Whistler calls his paintings of night and water Nocturnes, borrowing a musical title. Debussy takes the word back for his orchestra: his programme describes clouds fading through shades of grey and white.
cues.evidence: The connection to Whistler’s paintings and Debussy’s introductory programme are reproduced in the Los Angeles Philharmonic work note: https://www.laphil.com/works/nocturnes

cues.title: Two movements in Paris
cues.text: Camille Chevillard conducts Nuages and Fêtes in Paris on 9 December 1900. The third movement, Sirènes, waits nearly another year: the complete triptych reaches the stage on 27 October 1901.
cues.evidence: The two première dates, orchestra and conductor are documented in the IMSLP catalogue, https://imslp.org/wiki/Nocturnes_(Debussy,_Claude), and the Los Angeles Philharmonic note, https://www.laphil.com/works/nocturnes.

cues.title: Flute and harp together
cues.text: The middle passage moves to F♯ major. Flute and harp share a melody made from five notes, above strings held softly in many parts. Un peu animé — a little more animated — gives the tune a gentler forward swing.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, rehearsal 7, printed p. 13: six-sharp signature, flute and harp doubling the pentatonic melody, sustained divided strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The old phrase returns
cues.text: The cor anglais recovers its opening phrase. Debussy restores the first tempo, and the flute-and-harp tune falls away. The lower strings play near the fingerboard, softening the edge of their held notes.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, printed p. 16: 1er tempo, returning cor anglais phrase and lower strings marked sur la touche.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A few plucked notes
cues.text: Plus lent, then Encore plus lent: slower, then slower still. Bassoon and flute pick up scraps of the earlier phrases. Muted horns linger above the final plucked strings, with a soft timpani roll underneath.
cues.evidence: Fromont full score, final page, printed p. 18: the two slower markings, bassoon and flute fragments, muted horns, timpani and pizzicato strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Flute and harp let in light
transitions.to: B · Flute and harp in F♯
transitions.how: At Un peu animé, the score changes to six sharps. Flute and harp share the five-note melody in F♯ major; the divided strings hold a quiet chord underneath. The bass sustains while the tune moves freely above it, replacing the opening’s rocking wind chords.
transitions.evidence: Fromont full score, printed pp. 12–13, rehearsal 7. https://purl.dlib.indiana.edu/iudl/variations/score/BFJ7336

transitions.title: The cor anglais comes back
transitions.from: B · Flute and harp in F♯
transitions.how: The flute’s tune sinks and softens. At 1er tempo, the cor anglais restores its old phrase over held clarinet and bassoon notes. The key signature returns to two sharps. Violas, cellos and basses join quietly, bowing near the fingerboard.
transitions.evidence: Fromont full score, printed p. 16: 1er tempo, cor anglais, clarinet and bassoon support, and strings marked sur la touche.

transitions.title: The phrases break apart
transitions.to: Coda · Wind fragments and plucked strings
transitions.how: The cor anglais phrase shortens, and bassoons take up the rocking chords. The score slows twice, through Plus lent and Encore plus lent. Timpani hold the low B while the string bows stop; the final wind fragments sound above quiet pizzicato notes.
transitions.evidence: Fromont full score, printed pp. 17–18, including the two slower markings and final timpani and pizzicato writing.

source.title: Debussy, Nocturnes, original orchestral score, Kalmus reprint of Fromont
source.locator: Nuages, printed pp. 2–18: rocking clarinet and bassoon chords, flute and harp in F♯ major at rehearsal 7, the cor anglais return at 1er tempo, and the closing fragments.

timeline.note: Clarinets and bassoons rock between quiet chords.
The cor anglais phrase crosses held wind notes and muted violins, with soft timpani below.
Wind phrases rise over the strings as the orchestra swells.
The cor anglais recovers its narrow phrase above quieter strings.
Oboe and viola phrases stand out as the other instruments fall away.
Flute and harp share the five-note melody above held, divided strings.
Solo strings continue the middle section, with muted horns and harp beneath them.
The cor anglais returns, with the rocking clarinet and bassoon chords and softly held lower strings.
Cor anglais and bassoon phrases break into fragments over soft timpani and low strings.
Flute fragments, muted horns, quiet timpani and plucked strings carry the ending away.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande (orchestra), Ernest Ansermet (conductor)
fields.note: The instrumental movement has no choral part. No orchestral soloist or complete roster is identified or inferred. The unresolved Sirènes chorus does not enter this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Original orchestral work; exact performing edition unestablished
fields.note: The sources identify the work and movement, but not the parts or revision used in October 1951. The original Fromont/Kalmus and 1930 Jobert full scores were viewed. Musical annotations use shared principal passages; no claim that Ansermet follows every detail of the revised edition, no cut/repeat-order certification, and no bar-accurate score alignment. Orchestra states are explicitly provisional passage estimates, not audio instrument detection.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Month and year are corroborated. Stuart’s [a] Nocturnes has no exact day: the 10th and 12th in the shared session heading refer to other works. The 1951 session must not be described as a 1951 publication.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Venue is independently supplied by the session discography and the matching London CD catalogue record.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Original British LP label; London LL 530 is the separately dated June 1952 issue in Stuart.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: First British issue March 1952. Side A contains the three Nocturnes; side B Ravel’s Rapsodie espagnole. Original label images were not present in the IA item, so the date relies on the discography rather than an inspected LP label.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side A; suite master series SAR587–SAR592
fields.note: IA identifies the side and track order; Stuart assigns SAR587–92 to Nocturnes as a whole. No individual movement matrix, LP runout, take number or pressing identification is established, and none is extrapolated from the six-number series.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No digital-transfer engineer is credited. IA account identity is not a transfer credit. Victor Olof (producer) and Gil Went (engineer) are documented for the original Decca session, not for this digital transfer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item was uploaded/published on IA on 26 December 2021. That is not evidence for when the physical record was transferred.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Original FLAC and derived VBR MP3 are listed, but playback equipment, equalisation, de-clicking, noise reduction, pitch correction and intervening edits are undocumented. No listening or processing-quality claim is made.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public-domain underlying composition under ordinary life-plus-70 terms
fields.note: Debussy died in 1918; the original score was published in 1900–01. Original and 1930 score pages were consulted as historical score evidence. This assessment of the composition is separate from sound-recording rights and does not claim rights in a modern edition, scan or arrangement.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 territorial basis: EU sound recording first published before 1963; US public-domain status not established
fields.note: LXT 2637 was issued in March 1952, not 1951. Under the ordinary former EU 50-year publication term this predates expiry before the 1 November 2013 extension threshold. This is the project’s territorial pre-1963 basis, not a Creative Commons licence or a worldwide public-domain claim. US status has not been established. IA supplies no open-licence URL; the upload alone does not grant rights.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
